groups.instructions: The young people below all want to join a club during the summer holidays. On the right there are descriptions of eight clubs. For each question, choose the correct answer.

optionPool.title: Riverside Rowing
optionPool.text: Never been in a boat? Our coaches teach complete beginners on the calm river every Tuesday and Thursday from 6 pm. All equipment is provided.

optionPool.title: Stage Nights
optionPool.text: Bands and singers aged 13–17 rehearse together twice a week. At the end of August every group plays a concert in the town square.

optionPool.title: Art in the Park
optionPool.text: A large drawing class for all ages, every Sunday afternoon. Bring your own materials and draw whatever you like — there is no teacher.

optionPool.title: Hill Farm Helpers
optionPool.text: Spend your mornings feeding goats, cleaning out the stables and looking after the young animals at our family farm. Volunteers aged 12+ welcome.

optionPool.title: Small Studio
optionPool.text: Groups of no more than six young artists work with a professional illustrator. Classes are on Saturdays from 9.30 to 12.

optionPool.title: Film Lab
optionPool.text: Make your own film in a week! We lend cameras, microphones and editing laptops, and the best films are shown at our summer festival.

optionPool.title: Climbing Wall
optionPool.text: Experienced climbers can join our weekend competitions. You must already know how to use the safety equipment.

optionPool.title: Pet Care Course
optionPool.text: Learn how to look after cats, dogs and rabbits in a five-day course with a vet. Certificate included. Mornings, Monday to Friday.

parts.title: My year as a young reporter
parts.stimulusHtml:
Fifteen-year-old Nadia Reyes writes about working for her town's newspaper.

When our English teacher told us that the local newspaper wanted a teenager to write a weekly column, I nearly didn't apply. I had written stories for fun since I was small, but I had never shown them to anyone except my grandmother. In the end my best friend filled in the form with me, mostly so that I would stop talking about it.

My first article was about the new bus timetable, which I thought was a boring subject. The editor, Mr Patel, didn't change a single word, but he told me that the best articles answer the questions readers actually ask. So for my second article I stood at the bus station for an hour and asked people what they thought. I learnt more in that hour than in a week of reading about it online.

Not everything went well. In March I wrote about the school canteen and some parents were angry because they thought I had been unfair to the cooks. I was upset at first, but Mr Patel helped me write a reply, and the next week I interviewed the head cook. That article got more letters than anything I had written before — almost all of them kind.

Now I spend about four hours a week on the column. It isn't always easy to fit it in with homework, and my friends sometimes complain that I'm always asking them questions! But I've discovered that I'm good at listening, and I've started to think that journalism could be a real job for me one day.

groups.bodyHtml:
by Leo Brandt, aged 14

Last winter I decided that I wanted to learn to cook. {{q:16}} Until then I had only ever made toast!

At first I watched lots of videos online. {{q:17}} The recipes used ingredients I had never heard of, and the cooks did everything so fast that I couldn't follow them.

{{q:18}} He has been cooking for sixty years, so he seemed like the perfect teacher. He showed me how to make a simple vegetable soup, and the first time I made it on my own I was really proud. {{q:19}}

Not every meal has been a success. I once burnt a cake so badly that the kitchen was full of smoke. {{q:20}} Now my cakes are almost as good as my grandfather's!

optionPool.text: So I decided to ask my grandfather to teach me instead.
It tasted much better than anything I had made before.

groups.bodyHtml:
by Sofia Marin

Last term our class decided to do something about the rubbish in {{q:27}} local park. Every Saturday morning about twenty of us met at the gate {{q:28}} spent two hours collecting plastic bottles, paper and cans.

At first some people laughed at us, but soon other families {{q:29}} joining in. The town council was so pleased that it gave us money to buy new bins. Now the park is one {{q:30}} the cleanest places in town.

We learnt that you don't have to be an adult to change things. If you see a problem, don't wait {{q:31}} somebody else to fix it — do it {{q:32}}!
